beliefs.practice: Create a single Mongo client (MotorClient/MongoClient) instance at application startup and reuse it for all requests; do not create a new client per incoming HTTP request.
Read the cluster connection string from an environment variable (e.g., DOCUMENTDB_URI) or a secrets store at runtime and never commit credentials into source control or logs.
Enable TLS/SSL in the connection string and verify certificates (use tls=true/tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=false or the provider-recommended options) to ensure encrypted connections to the cluster.

Set sensible connection-pool and timeout parameters in the client URI (e.g., maxPoolSize, connectTimeoutMS, socketTimeoutMS, serverSelectionTimeoutMS) tuned for your app concurrency rather than relying on defaults.
Use least-privilege database credentials: create a dedicated DB user for the service with only the necessary roles/permissions (readWrite on the specific database), not the cluster admin account.

For tenant/partitioning, set a partition key (use customer_id as the collection/partition key) so reads and writes for a single customer are routed to a single partition and to avoid cross-partition scatter.

Model append-only consent history carefully: keep event arrays bounded (e.g., cap length or move older events to a separate history collection) to avoid unbounded single-document growth and the associated performance/memory issues.

Use single-document atomic updates when possible: update the current preference and append a history entry in the same document with a single update operator ($push and $set) to keep the document state consistent without multi-document transactions.
Create an index on customer_id (and any compound indexes for query patterns like customer_id + channel) to support fast lookups for reads that fetch a customer's current preferences.

Define TTL-based retention with a TTL index (expireAfterSeconds on a date field such as expiresAt or createdAt) to automatically delete documents older than the retention window; ensure the field is a proper BSON date and the index is created with expireAfterSeconds.

If you need to preserve an audit trail longer than a single document allows or to ensure immutable audit records, store history events in a separate collection (with their own indexes and TTL or archival process) instead of an ever-growing sub-array.

When creating indexes at runtime (ORM/ODM startup or seed), ensure index creation is idempotent and handled asynchronously at startup; do not block request handling on long index builds in production without monitoring.

Implement idempotency for write endpoints (e.g., idempotency key or use upsert with a deterministic id) so retries from clients or the service don't create duplicate events or inconsistent history entries.

Enable driver retryable writes and include client-side exponential backoff with bounded retries for transient network errors; make write operations idempotent where retries could otherwise duplicate work.

Avoid storing large binary blobs or extremely large arrays in documents (e.g., vector embeddings per customer inside the main consent doc). If using vectors, store them in a separate collection optimized for vector indexing/search.

If using the cluster's vector-search capability, create a proper vector index with explicit dimension, index type (HNSW/IVF), and metric; ensure the stored vector field is a fixed-length numeric array and queries include appropriate filter predicates (e.g., customer_id) to reduce search scope.
Use projection and pagination in read endpoints (limit/skip or ranged queries) to avoid returning entire history arrays; fetch only the current preferences or the last N history entries as needed.

When using an ODM like Beanie, call the ODM initialization routine (init_beanie) during app startup with explicit models and ensure index creation/migrations are controlled (do not rely on implicit index creation per-request).

Monitor and alert on key metrics: connection pool exhaustion, slow queries, index usage, request latency, and server selection/availability errors; enable database-level monitoring and collect driver logs in app telemetry.

Design for limited or no cross-partition multi-document transactions: avoid application designs that require transactions across many customer partitions; instead keep per-customer work within a single partition/document when possible.

Protect the management plane: restrict network access to the cluster with firewall rules or VNet integration and avoid exposing the database to wide public access from development machines where possible.

Validate and enforce schema at the application level (Beanie/Pydantic models) for consentVersion, channel names, and timestamp formats to prevent inconsistent documents being written; do not rely solely on client input.

For TTL-enforced retention of audit/history, prefer expiring the audit documents themselves (separate collection) rather than expiring customer records that might be needed for active service; ensure TTL removal timing/precision is acceptable for compliance.

When seeding sample data and creating indexes against a live cluster, run those operations from a controlled script that checks for and reports errors and does not alter other databases; make seed scripts idempotent and reversible where possible.
